analysis.one_liner: Gives families a fully refundable $3,000 yearly credit per child, paid monthly.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 187 House Democratic cosponsors — 81% of the caucus — but died in the Ways and Means Committee without ever receiving a vote in the House or Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the existing child tax credit with a larger, fully refundable one: $3,000 a year for each child ages 6 through 17 and $3,600 for each child under 6, with Treasury sending families part of it in monthly payments through the year. Because the credit would be fully refundable, the poorest families — who owe little or no income tax — would get the full amount. The bill included no offsetting revenue to pay for the cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Any family raising children under 18 would gain. Because the credit would be fully refundable, the biggest relative gains go to low-income families, who under current law receive little or nothing from the child tax credit because they owe little income tax. The bill also extends the benefit to families in Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories and adds a $500 credit for other dependents such as older teens or adult dependents. Households earning above the phase-out thresholds ($180,000 for married couples, $130,000 for singles) would see the new credit shrink.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families raising children, especially low-income families

how_it_helps.text: Raises the child tax credit to $3,000 per child ages 6 through 17 and $3,600 (120% of that) for each child under age 6.
Makes the credit fully refundable, so low-income families too poor to owe income tax would receive the full amount rather than only what their tax bill allows.
Requires Treasury to set up a program paying the credit out monthly during the year, giving families a steady stream of cash instead of one lump sum at tax time.
Increases the credit amounts each year with inflation starting after 2020, so the benefit would not erode over time.
Extends the benefit to residents of Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, and other U.S. territories, which are largely left out of the current child tax credit.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts, so the entire cost of the expanded credit would be absorbed by the federal Treasury through higher borrowing or general revenue. Households earning above the phase-out thresholds would also get a smaller credit than under the bill's headline amounts.

drawbacks.text: The bill is entirely unpaid for: it contains no tax increase or spending cut to offset the cost, so the full price lands on the federal deficit and general taxpayers.
Families whose income crosses the thresholds — $180,000 for married couples or $130,000 for single filers — would lose part or all of the expanded credit.

Monthly advance payments would have to be reconciled against the family's actual credit at tax time, and if the advances exceeded the final credit the family would owe the difference back as additional tax — a real risk for households whose income rises during the year.

The bill eliminates the existing child tax credit structure and replaces it, including replacing the current $500 non-refundable credit for non-child dependents, so some families' benefits would change rather than simply rise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families with children the benefit is large, direct, and concentrated on those with the least income, which is a strong argument on its own. The honest cost is that the bill has no funding mechanism, so it would add to the deficit, and the monthly advance system would create reconciliation headaches — including surprise repayments — for families whose circumstances change. A supporter would have needed to pair it with a revenue source and smooth out the advance-payment design.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the bill sat there — the committee that handles all tax legislation — without ever being reported out, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 6, 2019, and 187 House Democrats — 81% of the 231-member caucus — signed on as cosponsors.
No House Republican cosponsored the bill, and the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day it was introduced.
That referral was the bill's last recorded action: the committee never reported it and the full House never voted on it in either 2019 or 2020.
The bill died automatically when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021; bills not passed by then must start over from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal Treasury and general taxpayers avoided the cost of the expanded credit, and the existing child tax credit stayed as it was. Families with children — especially low-income families who would have gained the most from a fully refundable, monthly payment — received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury avoided the cost; families gained nothing

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 187 cosponsors, making it one of the most heavily cosponsored bills of the Congress.

for.name: 187 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Majority Leader and much of the caucus leadership.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill on referral; the committee never took it up, held no markup, and reported nothing out.

against.name: 197 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsor and no support for the bill, and it never reached a floor vote on which any member could vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 187 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber, so no roll call ever occurred.
